official.title: Doctoral Researcher / Master's Thesis Worker - VIcTOR - Virtual Torque Sensing for Maritime Powertrains
official.description_text:
The School of Engineering drives science and innovation in industrial and built environment technologies. We are committed to educating a new generation of experts who combine technical excellence with a deep understanding of sustainable development in shaping societies. Our research focuses on sustainable built environment, mechanics and materials, multidisciplinary energy technology, and design and implementation of technical systems. The strength of our school lies in close collaboration with stakeholders across research and education. About 45 doctoral candidates and 350 master’s students graduate from the school every year. The school is home to 700 staff members, including 70 professors. To learn more, please visit eng.aalto.fi.
School of Engineering is an international unit with nearly 70 talented professors and 3400 full-time students. Currently, the Department of Mechanical Engineering has 30 professors together with lecturers, post-doctoral researchers, doctoral students, and technical staff. In total, the number of personnel is about 300.
Aalto University Rotor Lab at the Department of Mechanical Engineering, in collaboration with our industrial partner Wärtsilä, is looking for a
Doctoral Researcher / Master's Thesis Worker
VIcTOR - Virtual Torque Sensing for Maritime Powertrains
Description of the project
Knowledge of the torque and torsional response of a maritime powertrain is important for emission-compliant control. Torque and torsional response are normally measured using strain gauges, dedicated torque sensors, or other instrumentation installed on the drivetrain. Torsional response can also be calculated if the external torsional forces acting on the powertrain are known, but measurements of this external forcing are rare in maritime powertrains. Instrumenting large maritime powertrains is also costly, and there is often not enough measured information available to fully determine the torsional response using conventional methods alone.
Unknown external forces and torsional response can instead be estimated using methods such as convex optimization or Kalman filtering. These torque estimation methods allow much more freedom in sensor placement and reduce the number of sensors needed to characterize the full torsional response of the powertrain.
This project aims to develop a torque estimation procedure that determines the unknown input torque and full torsional response using only encoder (speed, position) measurements together with selected available measurements from the driving internal combustion engine (e.g. cylinder pressure) or the driven electric generator (e.g. electromagnetic torque) — removing the need for an expensive, dedicated torque transducer.
Two complementary approaches will be explored. The first is convex optimization-based torque estimation, which allows constraints to be incorporated flexibly, both to keep estimated quantities physically consistent and to enforce desired structure in the results. The second is physics-informed learning, which combines available historical data with known system dynamics as a regulariser for data-driven learning — enabling nonlinear system dynamics to be learned indirectly with less training data than traditional data-driven approaches, for example to estimate the external torsional excitation from the propeller.
To ultimately remove the need for a torque flange, the estimation method must be integrated into the embedded engine control system. The work will make use of industry-standard tools such as Matlab Simulink to connect with existing control systems and support SIL/MIL simulation, and the resulting algorithm must run efficiently within the CPU constraints of an embedded system.
The project is carried out in collaboration with Wärtsilä, which provides powertrain data, operational torsional-dynamics measurements for model verification, and access to a physical maritime powertrain for validating the developed torque estimation procedure. You will be employed by the University, but your work will be conducted physically both at Aalto University campus and Wärtsilä Vaasa STH laboratory, to provide best-possible methodological support for your doctoral dissertation project.
Research focus
Defining the accuracy and operational requirements for the torque estimation algorithm
Building and verifying a torsional vibration model of the powertrain, based on data provided by Wärtsilä, with a final test environment in Simulink
Developing convex optimization-based and/or physics-informed deep learning approaches to torque estimation
Studying the torque estimation framework first with simulated measurements and scenarios, then verifying it against measurements from Wärtsilä's physical powertrain
Testing and refining the torque estimation model for implementation in an embedded environment with limited computing capacity
Skills we are looking for
Please note that these are considered assets, not strict requirements:
Background in mechanical engineering, control engineering, applied mathematics, electrical engineering, or a related field
Knowledge of torsional vibration, rotordynamics, or powertrain/drivetrain dynamics
Experience with state estimation or optimization methods (e.g. Kalman filtering, convex optimization)
Interest or experience in machine learning, particularly physics-informed or physics-constrained learning
Programming and modelling skills (Matlab/Simulink, Python, C or other embedded-systems languages)
Interest in embedded systems and control engineering, and in working with industrial measurement data
General eligibility criteria
Master's or Bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering, or other relevant field
Excellent written and oral skills in English
Finnish language skills are considered a benefit
Applicants must be able to work full-time and, for doctoral studies, meet the official eligibility requirements of the Aalto Doctoral Programme in Engineering during a trial period of 6 months:
aalto.fi/en/study-options/aalto-doctoral-programme-in-engineering
What we offer
Salary during Master's thesis phase: 2622 €/month (gross), full-time, max. 6 months, employment at Wärtsilä
After graduation, doctoral researcher starting salary: 3143 €/month (gross), with possible increases based on achievements
Annual workload: 1612 hours
Employment contract includes occupational health care; Finland has a comprehensive social security system
First doctoral contract: 2 years, followed by a midterm evaluation and extension for up to 4 years in total
Strong collaboration with Wärtsilä (access to engines, test rigs, operational data, and industry experts)
International and multidisciplinary research environment with excellent facilities

ai.summary: A 2-3 year doctoral position (or 6-month Master's thesis phase followed by PhD) in torque estimation for maritime powertrains using state estimation, optimization, and physics-informed learning, developed in collaboration with the maritime equipment manufacturer Wärtsilä.

thematic_fit.rationale: The position focuses on maritime powertrain dynamics, torque sensing, state estimation, and embedded control systems. The researcher's domain is human-centred XR, collaborative immersive systems, spatial learning, and wayfinding. There is no thematic connection.

methodological_fit.rationale: Both domains involve modeling and simulation (Simulink), but serve entirely different purposes. The position requires rotordynamics, convex optimization, Kalman filtering, and physics-informed machine learning applied to mechanical systems. The researcher's methods are user studies, experimental design for human performance, and XR application development. The only surface overlap is 'modeling' and 'ML interest,' which is insufficient for meaningful methodological transfer.

growth_value.rationale: This role would develop skills in state estimation, optimization, and embedded systems — valuable for robotics or control engineering, but orthogonal to human-centred XR research. It does not address the researcher's stated capability gaps (e.g., statistics, mixed-effects modeling for behavioral analysis, eye-tracking, physiological sensing in immersive contexts).

strategic_value.rationale: Aalto is a priority-1 institution with strong funding and industrial partnership (Wärtsilä). However, the research focus (maritime/mechanical engineering) diverges fundamentally from the researcher's target identity. The group (Rotor Lab, Mechanical Engineering) lacks expertise in HCI, immersive systems, or human-centred research. Supervisor Viitala specializes in rotordynamics, not human-computer interaction.

eligibility_flags: Position explicitly accepts Master's thesis worker (6 months) or doctoral researcher; researcher is in thesis stage — thesis-phase eligibility unclear but possible
Requires background in mechanical engineering, control engineering, applied mathematics, or related field; researcher's background is creative multimedia — significant disciplinary mismatch
Requires knowledge of torsional vibration, rotordynamics, or powertrain dynamics; researcher has none
Requires Matlab/Simulink, Python, or C; researcher has C# and Unity experience but not listed languages at required depth
Finnish language 'considered a benefit' but not required; researcher would likely need English-language support
risks: Strong disciplinary mismatch: creative multimedia background vs. mechanical/control engineering focus
No background in rotordynamics, state estimation, or optimization methods
Supervisor and industrial partner (Wärtsilä) focus on mechanical systems, not human-computer interaction or immersive learning
If pursued, PhD would diverge from target identity of human-centred XR researcher toward control systems and embedded engineering
Embedded systems work (C/Simulink) is further from researcher's XR/Unity development trajectory
